To summarize, the key findings of our research, stated in one sentence that includes all relevant information, are that
• The noise model is accurate for the range of supply voltages and process corners that are of interest for delay testing.

(a) power supply noise can be modeled as a Gaussian noise source with zero mean and standard deviation σ; (b) the standard deviation of the power supply noise is proportional to the square of the clock frequency; (c) the standard deviation σ of the power supply voltage can be estimated from the standard deviation of delay variations; and (d) the delay variations can be estimated by using the standard deviation of a test vector’s delay and the standard deviation of its power supply voltage.
• A new power supply noise model is proposed that is more accurate than existing models.

we have shown that the power grid noise is a major source of timing error in deep submicron technologies, and that it is necessary to include power noise in the timing models used to characterize and test these technologies.
we have proposed a new model for power noise in delay testing, which is more accurate than existing models and is much faster to calculate.
the proposed noise models can be used to estimate power supply noise in delay tests and can be applied to test compaction.

, in the presence of power supply noise, the delay of a circuit can be significantly different from its nominal value, which is the value measured under the assumption of noise-free power supply.
power supply noise can be modeled using the power supply current waveform, which is readily available in a delay test.
